title: Gesture
description: Gesture cinematography sizes and times a shot around a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a weight shift. The plot is in the motion, not in an object sitting still.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Sometimes the scene is not the face and not the prop, but the almost-touch, the glove tightening, the look that does not land. Gesture coverage treats that small action as the beat.
Duration matters: the movement has a start, a peak, and a settle. It is the wrong tool when the object is the fact (a key, a letter) rather than what the body does.
It is also the wrong tool as a wide master where fingers die in the noise of a room. Get close enough that the motion reads, then let it finish.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Frame for the moving part. Hands often want a close crop without becoming a product shot; a glance may live in a Close-Up of the eyes.
Keep the body connected enough that the motion has a source (wrist, shoulder). Light to separate fingers from background.
Prompt: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it when the plot is in the fingers: an almost-touch in a corridor, a glove, a glass that does not quite rise. Do not cover it so wide the motion dies, and do not freeze it into an object insert.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: An Insert Shot is usually the object as fact. A Close-Up is a size that may hold a gesture, or may hold a still face.
An Extreme Close-Up can be a fingertip as texture rather than as action. Gesture means the expressive movement is the subject.
If nothing moves, you probably wanted an insert.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: In the Mood for Love builds withheld romance out of hands, glances, and slow weight shifts more than out of speeches. Drive lets gloves, a wheel, and small body decisions carry threat.
Grammar: the small action is the line.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Name the movement. Example: Gesture close on [Subject], the meaning in a hand, a glance, a weight shift, coverage of the small action.
Say what the body does (fingers almost touching, a look away). For video, one motion with a settle; do not add a camera tour.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot of a still object, or a Close-Up of a face that never moves. The tell is a static prop hero, or a wide where the hand is a blur.
Fix: size to the moving part, let the action complete.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Gesture in film?

Gesture coverage is a shot sized and timed for a discrete expressive body movement: a hand, a glance, a shift of weight. The meaning is the action, not a still object and not a wide master of the room.
Gesture vs Insert Shot

An insert shows a story object or detail, often still enough to read as a fact. Gesture shows what a body does with or without that object. A key in the palm can be an insert; the hesitation before the hand closes is gesture.
When should I use Gesture?
Use it when the beat is a small body action the wide cannot prove. Do not use it for a still product-like object, and do not bury the motion in a master.
How do I prompt Gesture for AI image or video?
Write Gesture close on [Subject], and name the hand, glance, or weight shift. For video, describe one motion and a settle. Keep the camera still unless the technique is a move.
